claim: Measuring the same creator behaviour on a popularity-gated sample rather than a random sample of the platform inflates the estimate roughly tenfold: 36.7% versus 3.49% of How To & Style videos carrying affiliate links.
stance_target: Creator statistics drawn from established or self-selected populations systematically overstate the typical creator
scope_conditions: YouNiverse (channels with 10,000+ subscribers, English-speaking, late 2019) compared with Mathur et al.'s random-prefix sample of all YouTube videos; part of the gap is also attributable to a stricter affiliate-link definition in Mathur et al.
quoted_support: According to their measurements, for instance, 3.49% of How To & Style videos present affiliate marketing links (compared to 36.7% in our measurement). This large difference between our results can be explained in two ways.

claim: Among YouTube channels with at least 10,000 subscribers, 60.6% used at least one off-platform monetization strategy, appearing in 18.4% of all videos, meaning platform ad revenue alone does not describe how most established creators earn.
stance_target: Creator income is diversified off-platform, so platform payout data understates and misdescribes creator earnings
scope_conditions: 71,089,725 videos from 136,091 English-speaking channels, all with 10,000+ subscribers at collection in late 2019; detection based on monetization domains and crypto addresses in video descriptions
quoted_support: We find that, according to this criterion, 18.4% of the videos and 60.6% of the channels in the dataset have used at least one alternative monetization strategy

claim: Median LIFETIME Patreon income for the 97 YouTube channels observed with a Patreon link was USD 5,540, and median lifetime cryptocurrency donation income for 58 channels was USD 1,155.
stance_target: Off-platform fan funding produces small lifetime sums for most creators who use it
scope_conditions: 97 and 58 channels respectively, drawn from 497 Alt-lite/Alt-right/Manosphere 'problematic' channels - NOT a general creator sample; income measured via Graphtreon and public blockchain history to November 2020; the authors warn a linked Patreon or wallet may belong to someone other than the channel owner, so these are likely overestimates
quoted_support: Fig. 6. Problematic channel income (a) from Patreon (97 channels), median income 5540 US dollars, (b) Bitcoin and Ethereum (58 channels), median income 1155 US dollars.
numbers: 68 of 97 channels earned over USD 1,000 lifetime on Patreon
30 of 58 earned over USD 1,000 in crypto
Honey Badger Radio over USD 260,000 across six years

claim: Adoption of off-platform monetization scales strongly with channel size and output: 72% of the most productive decile of channels use it versus 30% of the least productive decile, and top-decile channels post merchandise links at 12.5% versus 3.6% for the bottom decile.
stance_target: Access to diversified revenue is concentrated among already-successful creators
scope_conditions: Deciles computed within a sample already floored at 10,000 subscribers, so the 'bottom decile' here (under 12.7k subscribers) is still far above the platform median creator
quoted_support: among the least productive 10% of the channels (left-most bar), who produced at most 29 videos, only 30% adopt alternative monetization. The adoption rate is much higher among more prolific channels. Over 72% of the most productive 10% of the channels (right-most bar) include alternative monetization links

claim: In a matched-pair design of 5,730 channel pairs, channels that adopted off-platform monetization posted 63 videos over the following year versus 44 for matched non-adopters, a 43% increase in output.
stance_target: Whether monetization drives creator persistence and output, or merely accompanies it
scope_conditions: Channels matched on content category and on both view-decile and video-decile for three consecutive months before adoption; adoption months January 2015 to September 2019; top 5% by output and views excluded; the authors explicitly decline a causal interpretation
quoted_support: Over the entire year, aggregating the number of videos produced between months 1 to 12, channels adopting alternative monetization strategies produced 63 videos on average while those who did not produced 44 videos. This amounts to an increase in productivity of over 43%.

claim: Off-platform fan funding severs the link between views and earnings, so a creator with few views can out-earn a high-view creator if a small dedicated audience pays, which invalidates view counts and subscriber counts as proxies for creator income.
stance_target: Audience-size metrics cannot be used to infer creator income
scope_conditions: Authors' interpretation, grounded in their own adoption measurements; references Kevin Kelly's '1,000 True Fans' framing
quoted_support: Even if videos created by some creators receive only a few views, they can amass substantial earnings if a small but dedicated set of fans are willing to pay for a subscription.

claim: The most widely used creator research dataset for YouTube is restricted to English-speaking channels with over 10,000 subscribers, so the published academic literature on YouTube creators structurally excludes both small creators and non-English-speaking regions.
stance_target: Western/anglophone bias is built into the underlying data, not just the interpretation
scope_conditions: YouNiverse dataset construction; the authors note the United States accounts for under 20% of YouTube traffic
quoted_support: YouNiverse: A dataset comprised of 71,089,725 videos from 136,091 English-speaking YouTube channels ... All channels in the dataset had at least 10,000 subscribers when data collection happened.
numbers: US is under 20% of YouTube traffic
region: English-speaking channels only; explicitly not generalisable to Southeast Asia
